headline: Institutional capital flows favouring APAC and Europe over US, benefiting Qualitas' geographic expansion strategy
reasoning: Schwartz notes that among global institutional capital flows, APAC and Europe are the two most favoured destinations, with the US losing share. Qualitas is currently focused on Australia and Europe, positioning it as a beneficiary of this capital flow trend. The firm's European expansion via the acquisition of Starz — a private credit business with 10 staff and 11 investments across the UK and pan-Europe — is intended to grow the addressable market by roughly fivefold. Schwartz views the European business as a medium-term proposition that could eventually rival the Australian business in revenue and profit contribution.
quote: And if you look at institutional capital flows, APAC and Europe are the two most favoured destinations. Unfortunately it's coming at the expense of the United States. But at the moment we are focused on Australia and Europe. So where the beneficiary of that as well. And when does Europe become sort of financially material to quality's? Look, I think we're in the building phase of it obviously, you know, we're a large and growing business in in Australia. And for us, you know, the first step is raising that institutional capital so that we can, you know, take their transaction flow forward. And, you know, I think it's a medium term proposition for us to really grow it and for it to rival the Australian business. But I do believe that in time it will rival our business in Australia and be a very material component of the total revenue and profits of the firm.
episode_title: Can Qualitas' numbers rewrite the private credit narrative?

headline: Qualitas argues market is confusing real estate cycle with credit cycle, obscuring strong deployment growth
reasoning: Andrew Schwartz believes the market underestimates Qualitas because investors conflate softness in the residential real estate market with weakness in private credit, when the two cycles are driven by different factors. Private credit dynamics are governed by bank behaviour, supply of competing capital, and the interest rate cycle — not property prices. Qualitas deployed $6.5 billion in the last 12 months, up ~40% on the prior year, and opened the current year with $1.1 billion of investment committee-approved or closed transactions, one of the strongest starts in the firm's history. Schwartz contends that once investors properly distinguish the credit cycle from the real estate cycle, the underlying business strength becomes apparent.
quote: Look, I think the main thing the market seems to me is about qualities is it gets confused between what I would call is the real estate cycle versus the credit cycle. So obviously investors in Australia are very aware of the softness of the residential market, particularly since the budget changes, three interest rate hikes later. And so they feel that because there's underlying softness in that market that that must be feeding into those that are providing private credit into that market. My argument is private credit is a totally different cycle to the real estate cycle. Private credit is much more about what the bank's behavior is at any point in time. It's about what your supply of capital is into the market that's providing competition for the capital. It's about the interest rate cycle. And I think that just generally investors get confused between the real estate cycle and the credit cycle. So I really try to emphasize that, particularly when you look at our results and you see, you know, we deployed $6.5 billion of capital in the last 12 months. You know, that was up some 40% on the the prior year. And, you know, we announced that we opened this year with $1.1 billion of either investment committee approved or closed transactions, one of the strongest openings that I can recall in our operating history.
episode_title: Can Qualitas' numbers rewrite the private credit narrative?

headline: Qualitas CEO highlights redemption and leverage risks afflicting retail-facing global private credit peers as a structural sector risk
reasoning: Schwartz identifies two key structural risks that have caught global private credit peers: back leverage in funds (where external lenders can call in loans during stress) and retail or high-net-worth redemption exposure where investors expected 30-90 day liquidity from fundamentally illiquid assets. He contrasts this with Qualitas's model, which uses no back leverage and has only ~1% of fee-earning FUM exposed to 90-day redemption rights, presenting the firm's structure as a competitive differentiator. The implicit warning is that investors in the broader private credit sector should scrutinise capital source stability and redemption terms.
quote: For somebody like qualities we've got really two distinct advantages. One is the fact that we have no back leverage. So we have which means we haven't taken loans and put them into our funds themselves. So what that means is that if it was to be a particularly bad period in, in the Australian market, and I'm being hypothetical in that statement, you know, we're not going to find a lender, external lender knocking on our door saying we'd like to call in the loan in your funds that you've on leant into into the industry. So we're dealing with equity capital. It's very stable. The other real competitive advantage is as an institutional provider of capital we don't expose ourselves to. Redemption issues, which is really a big issue that's going on globally at the moment, where you've seen some of those, you know, large global peers who have had more retail based money or high net worth money, who, you know, thought they could have access to their capital within 90 days, sometimes even earlier 30 days, and have been seeking to withdraw the capital for what is fundamentally a non liquid asset class within the fund.
episode_title: Can Qualitas' numbers rewrite the private credit narrative?

headline: Qualitas CEO Andrew Schwartz flags 20% FY27 earnings growth is sustainable, underpinned by higher starting FUM and construction loan drawdowns
reasoning: Qualitas begins FY27 with fee-earning FUM already 20% higher than the start of FY26, providing strong earnings visibility. Construction lending creates a compounding effect as monthly drawdowns continuously increase fee-earning FUM throughout the year. The firm holds $2.4 billion in dry powder, giving approximately one year of runway without needing to raise new capital mid-transaction. Management's 18-year track record of uninterrupted deployment growth and zero capital losses in credit funds underpins confidence in the guidance range of $74-80 million normalised NPBT, representing up to 26% growth. The fund structure — no back leverage and minimal retail redemption exposure (only ~1% of fee-earning FUM subject to 90-day redemption rights) — is seen as a structural competitive advantage through market cycles.
quote: The beauty of a fund manager, such as qualities is the fact that every year we start with higher fee earning fund than we did have the previous, the previous year. So we're starting this financial year with 20% higher fee earning Fum. Also, as you just pointed out in the introduction, we do a lot of construction lending, which, you know, involves us drawing down every single month more funds to the borrowers for the construction projects. And every time we draw down more capital where our fee earning fund continues to increase month or month. So we're able to really look at forward forward guidance and really take take a view on that higher fee earning Fum, but also the commitments we made in previous periods, knowing we're going to continue to draw down under those construction loans.
episode_title: Can Qualitas' numbers rewrite the private credit narrative?

headline: Qualitas expands into European private credit via acquisition of Starz platform, targeting a fivefold increase in addressable market through revenue diversification
reasoning: Schwartz explains the European expansion as a deliberate revenue diversification strategy to reduce reliance on the Australian real estate market alone. Qualitas identified and acquired Starz, an existing private credit business with a team of ten and 11 investments across UK and pan-European markets, gaining access to an established track record and institutional investor base. The European market is characterised as a preferred destination for global institutional capital, consistent with Qualitas's core institutional model. Management believes the Australian playbook — institutional capital, no leverage, no retail redemptions — can be transplanted into the European market effectively.
quote: For us it was about our revenue diversification as much as anything else so that, you know, our entire story is not tied to, you know, the the Australian real estate market, albeit, you know, I love the country. And, you know, I think that the prospects are solid going forward. But I think notwithstanding anyone's particular bias or view, that you really do need to have revenue diversification there. And and so we've been looking for quite a long time. We found, uh, a private credit business that was known by the name of Starz, and it had an existing team of ten people, 11 investments spread across UK and pan pan Europe. And I felt that we were really getting involved in their track record. We were able to bring institutional capital that has really well looked after qualities over the years, and also take advantage of their institutional investors as well.
episode_title: Can Qualitas' numbers rewrite the private credit narrative?

headline: Qualitas CEO sees Australian residential property as structurally undersupplied, creating durable tailwinds for private credit alternative financiers
reasoning: Andrew Schwartz argues that Australia's residential property market remains structurally undersupplied, which generates sustained deal flow and attractive risk-adjusted returns for institutionally backed alternative lenders like Qualitas. He characterises Australia as 'one of the shining lights globally' for institutional private credit capital, alongside APAC and Europe. Global institutional investors continue to be attracted to the Australian market, supporting Qualitas's ongoing capital-raising efforts.
quote: Australia, APAC and and Europe are favoured destinations for institutional capital, for for private credit. And I think that our track record really stands solid for 18 years. You know not notwithstanding, you know, we've seen a lot over the period since we started the firm. You know, we've worked through, uh, uh, geopolitics, rising interest rates, Covid, falling interest rates, changes now to tax tax policies. And notwithstanding that, you know, we've had 18 years of uninterrupted deployment growth.
episode_title: Can Qualitas' numbers rewrite the private credit narrative?
